title_full: Symphony No. 2 in D major, Op. 36

composer.name: Ludwig van Beethoven
composer.nationality_note: Grove opens the article “German composer” (b Bonn, bap. Dec 17, 1770; d Vienna, March 26, 1827), and this set follows Grove. The label names the German cultural and linguistic nation, not a state: no German nation-state existed until 1871. Beethoven was born in Bonn, seat of the Electorate of Cologne — an Imperial state of the Holy Roman Empire, styled “of the German Nation” — and lived in Vienna from 1792 until his death. Across the composers in this set Grove's nationalities track the modern state that now holds the birthplace: Bonn and Hamburg give German (Beethoven, Brahms), Salzburg Austrian (Mozart), St Petersburg Russian (Shostakovich). Grove states no editorial rule for this, and does not always assign a nationality at all — Leopold Mozart, born in Augsburg, is simply “Composer, violinist and theorist”.

era_note: Kept Classical deliberately (decided 21 Aug 2026). periods.json buckets by year and the bucket sets the card colour; Romantic begins 1830, so all nine read Classical. The boundary is global, so moving it to split Beethoven would carry Haydn's late symphonies and the whole of Schubert across with him. Grove's three periods (first to c1802, second to c1812, third 1813-27) divide the nine 1-2 | 3-8 | 9, so the scholarly break falls at the Eroica, not at any date in the 1830s. This one sits in the first period, where the Classical label is uncontroversial.

place.polity_note: Before 11 August 1804 there is no Austrian Empire: the sovereign entity is the composite Habsburg Monarchy, and the Archduchy of Austria sits within the Holy Roman Empire. The historical basemap labels these lands “Austrian Empire” in its 1783 and 1800 snapshots regardless, which is why the card takes its wording from here and not from the map data.
place.note: Then a village north of Vienna, now a city district. Grove places Beethoven at Heiligenstadt from spring 1802, 'perhaps with the thought of spending longer in the country than usual for the sake of his health and hearing'.

reason.summary: Written at Heiligenstadt the summer his deafness became undeniable.
reason.occasion: No commission. Finished in the country retreat where he wrote the Heiligenstadt Testament that October.
reason.occasion_spoken: nobody but himself, alone with his deafness outside Vienna
reason.detail: Grove dates the Heiligenstadt Testament 6–10 October 1802 and reads it as 'a trough of despondency in his fluctuating moods'. The symphony is the large public work of that same summer — Grove notes it is 'among the more conservative works' despite 'its great advance in assurance over the First', and that in it 'Beethoven for the first time really engaged with the symphony orchestra'.

first_performance.notes: Grove gives the date. Wikipedia supplies the venue and the rest of the programme: the Third Piano Concerto and the oratorio Christus am Oelberge, both also premieres.

instrumentation.note: 8 wind, 4 brass, timpani and the five string parts. Trumpets and timpani play in the first, third and fourth movements only. Counted from the score's distinct parts, doublings once. Grove's work-list gives composition dates, first performances, publication and dedications but no instrumentation, so the count rests on Wikipedia's instrumentation section alone and is uncorroborated.

listen_for.hook: The minuet is gone — this is his first symphonic scherzo.
listen_for.spoken: the third movement, where the minuet is gone and his first symphonic scherzo takes its place
listen_for.detail: The first of the nine to head its third movement Scherzo outright, abandoning the minuet the Classical symphony had assumed.

listen_for.hook: Two notes, F sharp and G, quietly hold the whole thing together.
listen_for.detail: Grove singles out its 'inspired play with the notes F♯ and G as a means of unifying the whole' — an early instance of the thematic unification the Fifth would make famous.

listen_for.hook: The jokes in the outer movements offended the critics.
listen_for.detail: Wikipedia notes the scherzo and finale 'shocked the sensibilities of many contemporary critics'.

unknowns: How much of the symphony predates the move to Heiligenstadt in spring 1802.

No premiere roster survives: neither Grove nor Wikipedia gives player numbers for the 5 April 1803 Theater an der Wien concert, so the card counts the score's parts instead of the players on the platform.

Beethoven's birth date is not recorded. Grove gives the baptism — bap. 17 December 1770 — and `composer.born_date` carries that, which is the standard proxy and at most a day or two early. It is only ever used to date his age in the script, and no plausible birth date moves that age.
